title: 'A huge opportunity': Literary community ecstatic after P.E.I. author's Giller Prize win
summary: After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.

image.caption: Margaret Atwood, left, poses for a photo with P.E.I.'s Nicholas Herring after he won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday. (CBC)

blocks.text: PEI·New
After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.
Nicholas Herring took home $100K prize Monday for his novel Your Breath in Charcoal
Nicholas Herring won the $100,000 2026 Giller Prize, the top award for fiction in the country, for his second novel, Your Breath in Charcoal.
The author said he's relishing the opportunity the prize presents, and he's now figuring out his next steps.
"I just didn't think I was going to win so, yeah, I was quite shocked. I'm still quite shocked," Herring said.
"I got to twirl Margaret Atwood around on stage so, I mean, what do you say to that, right?... It's like a fever dream or something, you know? It's pretty awesome."
Island book lovers are big fans of 2026 Giller Prize winner Nicholas Herring
Aside from being an accomplished author, the native of Murray Harbour is also a carpenter and a fisherman.
Your Breath in Charcoal is his followup to 2022's Some Hellish, which won the Atwood Gibson Writers' Trust Fiction Prize.
Heather Doran, assistant manager at Bookmark in Charlottetown, said the business has been a longtime supporter of Herring's work.
She called Your Breath in Charcoal "a masterpiece" story about two Islanders who move to Toronto to work in the trades, and said Herring's Giller Prize win is "huge for writing on P.E.I."
"I think people forget that there's really good authors here because we're so small, and I think it's a great chance to put the Island writers on the map," Doran said.
"Last night in the ceremony, he said he had lots of books in him and we're greedy to always have a great book, so we can hardly wait to see what he does next."

Avid reader Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark in Charlottetown on Tuesday picking up her copy of Your Breath in Charcoal, the Giller Prize-winning novel by P.E.I. author Nicholas Herring. (Barry Acton/CBC)
Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark on Tuesday picking up the novel, which the avid reader said has been on her radar for a while.
After hearing the news of Herring's win Tuesday morning, she headed out to pick up her copy.
"When he decided to write this book, he said swing for the fences," Wonnacott said.
"I just thought what a beautiful metaphor for life … [and] just a reminder that ordinary people can do extraordinary things."

blocks.text: P.E.I. Writers' Guild executive director Shawn Hogan said it can't be overstated how important Herring's win is to P.E.I. storytelling, and that having an Islander recognized on such a grand scale is a "massive achievement."

"He would do it regardless of accolades, regardless of that kind of recognition, so I think that more than anything is more inspiring to other writers that are just true writers at their heart, and that's what he is," Hogan said.
"I think it's going to have a tremendous impact that I don't even know if he would be aware of what it's going to do for Island storytelling for years to come."

Since the win, Herring said his calendar has been getting pretty full with multiple talks and appearances planned.
He hopes to say something inspirational, and said he has a consistent message to impart: "You don't need permission to write a book."
"If you want to do it, go do it," Herring said.
"If I can write a book and win the Giller Prize, then you can, too. Like, it's that simple."
